record.title: VA-Bench measures the gap between spatial diagnosis and successful robot action
record.summary: Zhang et al. introduce VA-Bench, a simulator benchmark requiring general-purpose multimodal models to use RGB-only demonstrations, actively choose camera views, issue metric Cartesian robot commands and revise actions from execution feedback. Across 14 base task families and 12 primary model conditions, the authors report three runs over the same 20 physically verified seeds per task. The strongest tested condition has a three-run macro-average terminal task success of 53.93±3.17%, despite 100.0% target localization and 78.9% spatial-relation scores in its annotated run. In one matched active-camera versus passive five-view comparison, success rises from 27.86% to 57.50%; this comparison covers four model conditions and does not identify whether view relevance, cross-view integration or longer visual context explains the gain. No tested model completes the strict five-object long-horizon episode. These are author-reported benchmark results, not an independent reproduction.

evidence_gaps.description: VA-Bench results and the active/passive comparison have not been independently executed.
The simulator task set and one five-object composition family do not establish open-set or real-robot transfer.

brief.importance_rationale: If the benchmark’s patterns reproduce, the separation between high-level spatial diagnosis and successful closed-loop manipulation would materially affect how embodied models and active sensing are evaluated. This is a simulator benchmark with finite task families and author-reported experiments; its relevance is notable for evaluation design, not evidence of general real-world robot capability.
limitations: All measurements are author-reported simulator results; no independent execution was performed.
The annotated behavioral diagnostics use one run per condition; terminal success is repeated across three runs.
The active/passive protocol comparison is limited to four model conditions and combines possible view relevance, cross-view integration and context-length effects.
Held-out geometry/layout variants are finite and do not establish arbitrary open-set or real-robot generalization.
The strict long-horizon result covers one five-object composition family.
The paper does not intervene on perception, planning and execution components to identify which causes each observed failure.
brief.summary: Zhang et al. introduce VA-Bench, a simulator benchmark requiring general-purpose multimodal models to use RGB-only demonstrations, actively choose camera views, issue metric Cartesian robot commands and revise actions from execution feedback. Across 14 base task families and 12 primary model conditions, the authors report three runs over the same 20 physically verified seeds per task. The strongest tested condition has a three-run macro-average terminal task success of 53.93±3.17%, despite 100.0% target localization and 78.9% spatial-relation scores in its annotated run. In one matched active-camera versus passive five-view comparison, success rises from 27.86% to 57.50%; this comparison covers four model conditions and does not identify whether view relevance, cross-view integration or longer visual context explains the gain. No tested model completes the strict five-object long-horizon episode. These are author-reported benchmark results, not an independent reproduction.

technical.claimed_result: In one matched comparison, active camera control raised task success from 27.86% to 57.50% relative to passive input containing five predefined views. The paper reports the comparison for four conditions; it does not isolate view relevance, cross-view integration or longer visual context as the cause.
technical.demonstrated_result: The paper reports 14 base task families (11 single-arm, three dual-arm), seven held-out geometry/layout variants and one five-object long-horizon composition track. Twelve primary model conditions were evaluated in three runs over the same 20 physically verified seeds per base task. The strongest reported condition averaged 53.93±3.17% terminal success; in its annotated run it scored 100.0% on target localization and 78.9% on spatial relations. No model completed a strict long-horizon episode. These are author-reported simulator results.
technical.implementation_status: The paper links a public benchmark and code repository. The repository was not audited or executed, and results were not independently rerun in this activation.
technical.mechanism: VA-Bench requires the model to learn task procedure from RGB-only demonstrations, choose camera viewpoints, estimate metric robot–object geometry, issue Cartesian targets through a fixed model-agnostic controller, then revise from execution outcomes. It withholds privileged object poses, oracle trajectories and learned action heads.
technical.novelty: Connects active visual evidence acquisition, demonstration-conditioned spatial re-grounding, metric action and feedback revision in a single evaluated loop, with terminal success and trajectory-level diagnostics.
technical.regime: A fixed simulated robot-manipulation suite with RGB observations, metric action commands and 20 verified seeds per base task. Primary terminal-success results use three runs per model condition; the trajectory diagnostics use one fully annotated run per condition. The long-horizon track composes five objects in one simulator task family.
technical.reproducibility: The paper provides task/protocol descriptions, seed counts, repeated-run summaries and linked code. Independent execution, simulator/annotation audit and new-task transfer remain open.
technical.strongest_baseline: For active evidence acquisition, the paper compares camera control with passive observation that supplies five predefined views at each observation while preserving the same seeds, demonstrations, robot execution and terminal-success accounting. It also reports held-out geometry/layout transfer against the base-task regime.

brief.title: VA-Bench measures the gap between spatial diagnosis and successful robot action
brief.why_it_matters: The benchmark separates describing or locating objects from acquiring useful visual evidence, grounding metric actions and completing manipulation. Its reported gap between strong intermediate diagnostics and terminal success, plus the bounded active/passive comparison, gives embodied-agent evaluation a way to test the full observe–reason–act–revise loop rather than perception alone. The simulator, finite task families and untested real-robot transfer limit generalization.
